lesson.title: Magnitude and Phase: The Full Picture of a Spectrum
lesson.summary: Spectrum is the general idea of describing a signal by its frequency content, and a complete spectral description needs two companion pictures, a magnitude spectrum showing how large each frequency component is and a phase spectrum showing how it is shifted in time relative to a reference.
lesson.body:
The word spectrum shows up all over science and engineering, from the electromagnetic spectrum sorted by wavelength to the audio spectrum sorted by pitch. In every case it means the same thing: take a quantity, break it down by frequency, and lay the pieces out in order. In circuits, the frequency spectrum you just met, amplitude plotted against frequency, is the most common picture, but it is only half the story. Each harmonic in a Fourier series actually carries two independent pieces of information, a cosine coefficient an and a sine coefficient bn, and plotting only the combined amplitude Cn throws away information about exactly where in its cycle that harmonic sits relative to the others.

The fix is a well known trigonometric identity. Any sum of a cosine and a sine at the same frequency can be written as a single cosine with an amplitude and a phase shift: an cos(n omega0 t) + bn sin(n omega0 t) = Cn cos(n omega0 t - phi_n), where Cn = the square root of (an squared plus bn squared), and phi_n = the arctangent of (bn divided by an). Cn is what the frequency spectrum plots. phi_n is the piece that a magnitude-only spectrum leaves out, and a full spectral description of a signal pairs a magnitude spectrum (Cn versus frequency) with a phase spectrum (phi_n versus frequency).

Here is a fully worked, self contained example of the conversion. Suppose the fundamental component of some waveform has a1 = 3 V and b1 = 4 V. Then C1 = the square root of (3 squared plus 4 squared) = the square root of 25 = 5 V, and phi_1 = arctan(4/3) = 53.13 degrees. Check it by expanding the other way: 5 cos(x - 53.13 degrees) = 5 cos(x) cos(53.13 degrees) + 5 sin(x) sin(53.13 degrees) = 5(0.6) cos(x) + 5(0.8) sin(x) = 3 cos(x) + 4 sin(x), which is exactly a1 cos(x) + b1 sin(x) with a1 = 3 and b1 = 4. So this component shows up as a single 5 V line at the fundamental frequency on the magnitude spectrum, and a 53.13 degree point at the same frequency on the phase spectrum. The magnitude alone would tell you a component of 5 V exists at that frequency; the phase tells you exactly how it lines up in time with every other harmonic, which matters enormously once you add all the harmonics back together, since shifting even one harmonic's phase can change a waveform's shape completely while leaving every harmonic's magnitude untouched.

One more accurate but brief point worth knowing at this level: instruments and textbooks usually show only positive frequencies, called a one sided spectrum, since that is what a real measurement naturally produces. The complex exponential form of the Fourier series, a more advanced but equivalent bookkeeping method, technically splits each real sinusoidal component into a pair of half amplitude pieces sitting at plus and minus that frequency. For a real signal these two pieces are mirror images of each other in magnitude, so no information is gained or lost, it is purely a different way of organizing the same spectrum. Between the Harmonic Content chapter, the Frequency Spectrum chapter, and this one, you now have the full toolkit: which harmonics exist, how large each one is, and how each one is phased, all sorted by frequency exactly as the word spectrum promises.
